critical_unknowns: Is the pilot affordable at committed cash levels within the set-aside amount?
Does the revised offer actually express and prove the business's WHY, or is it only a tactical change?
What retention will the pilot cohort show, and will that be available before a scale decision?
Is the measured baseline conversion stable enough to compare against the pilot?
Which customer group is the belief-aligned early-adopter segment for this offer?
decisive_arguments: Option B best expresses inside-out decision-making: test a revised offer with a defined belief, defined proof, and defined early-adopter group before asking the broader market to respond.
Option C is the weakest fit because broad launch scales the WHAT before the WHY is evidenced; the brief supplies only a baseline conversion fact and leaves retention unknown.
Option A protects the measured baseline but provides no learning about whether the revised offer is more purpose-aligned or more trustworthy.

The pilot should not be treated as a generic conversion experiment: its value depends on pre-registering why the revised offer exists, which customer belief it serves, and what result would justify scale.

framework_applications.application: Use WHY-HOW-WHAT sequencing on the pilot: state the belief the revised offer is meant to prove, define the observable behaviors that deliver it, and make the offer itself the proof. The pilot should test whether customers respond to that belief, not only whether the changed WHAT converts.

Scale only after belief-aligned early adopters validate the revised offer. A pilot is the appropriate diffusion step before a broad launch because it creates evidence with the people most likely to reveal whether the change carries the WHY.

Filter A, B, and C through trust and loyalty, not short-term conversion alone. B passes conditionally because a well-designed pilot can strengthen alignment; C fails because it scales before alignment is evidenced; A is acceptable only as a deliberate pause when the pilot cannot be funded.

cards.minority_position: If the pilot cannot be funded within the set-aside, I would prefer A over an unbudgeted B or a premature C; a purpose-aligned business should not prove its belief by breaking its own financial guardrails.

option_scores.rationale: Keeping the current offer preserves the measured baseline and avoids unfunded spend, but it treats the baseline as enough. From a WHY-alignment view, it forgoes a bounded chance to learn whether the revised offer better proves the business's belief, so it is safe but incomplete.

A bounded pilot is the best fit for inside-out sequencing: it can test whether the revised offer proves the same purpose to belief-aligned early customers before scale. It is conditional because the brief leaves financial feasibility unresolved and the pilot must be designed as a purpose-and-retention test, not merely a conversion tactic.

Broad launch is WHAT-first scaling. With the revised offer untested for purpose alignment and pilot retention unknown, a broad launch risks spending at scale on a change that may optimize short-term conversion while weakening trust and loyalty. It also conflicts with the unresolved affordability constraint.

cards.strongest_objection: The pilot can become a dressed-up delay. If the revised offer is merely a tactical change with no meaningful purpose claim, or if the pilot lacks pre-registered purpose and retention measures, B adds cost and time without producing decision-grade learning. The unresolved financial-feasibility question makes that risk sharper.

cards.change_my_mind: I would move from B to C if the financial-feasibility check clears and the pilot meets a pre-registered conversion and retention threshold. I would move from B to A if the pilot cannot be funded within the set-aside or if retention instrumentation cannot be built before launch.

conditions.description: Set explicit conversion and retention thresholds in advance that would justify a broad launch after the pilot.
conditions.verification_method: Decision-owner reviews and records the scale-or-stop rule before pilot results are read.

Whether the pilot is affordable at committed cash levels remains unresolved.

decisive_arguments: The pack's Instinct material treats a gradual stroll as valid when the terrain is unfamiliar and the cost has been counted; a bounded pilot is the appropriate stroll before a broad launch.
The current offer has a measured baseline, so a pilot can compare increase against that baseline rather than relying on copied strategy or excitement about the revised offer.
A broad launch would be a jump without sufficient jungle-sniffing because pilot cohort retention is not yet measured and financial feasibility is unresolved.
Keeping the current offer avoids risk but also refuses learning; it leaves the organization with the same baseline and the same unanswered questions.
The pilot must be an execution assignment, not a trophy activity: named owner, measurement window, retention metric, budget check, and pre-registered pull trigger.

framework_applications.application: Use the Instinct Alignment System logic: recognize the current rhythm, sniff the pilot terrain before barking, and pair the sensed opportunity in the revised offer with verifiable evidence. The pilot is a controlled stroll, not a permanent delay.

Apply the Instinct-Intellect Execution Standard before committing spend: define the business outcome, baseline, success metric, owner, constraints, and red-line risks. The pilot should have an explicit scale-or-stop decision rule tied to conversion and retention.

option_scores.rationale: Keeping the current offer protects the measured baseline, but it treats a sensed opportunity as a cage. It produces no new evidence on the revised offer and leaves the key retention unknown untouched.

A bounded pilot is the strongest fit for instinct plus intellect: it tests the revised offer against the baseline while limiting exposure. It is conditional because the pilot must fit the set-aside and must measure retention, not just conversion.

A broad launch is a jump before the terrain has been sniffed. Retention is unmeasured and affordability at committed cash levels is unresolved, so broad launch would convert uncertainty into committed exposure.

cards.strongest_objection: A pilot can become a comfortable cage that produces activity without increase. If the pilot lacks a pre-registered retention metric, a hard budget check, and a clear scale-or-stop trigger, B merely delays the decision and may create false confidence.

cards.change_my_mind: I would move toward Option C only if measured pilot results showed both improved conversion against the baseline and adequate cohort retention, with participant treatment documented and the served group clearly identified; and I would move toward Option A if the purpose statement could not be written without becoming self-serving, if affordability at committed cash levels failed, or if a small cohort would treat people as subjects with no real intent to learn from them.

conditions.description: Write down the purpose of the revised offer in one paragraph: the problem it solves, who it is meant to serve, and what we would refuse to do to make it succeed. No pilot spend until this exists.

conditions.responsible_role: offer owner with the seat's owned question as the review lens
conditions.verification_method: The written purpose statement is reviewed and retained with the pilot plan, and it names the served group and at least one explicit non-goal.

required_evidence: Recorded resolution of the financial-feasibility question at committed cash levels
conditions.verification_method: The financial-feasibility check is recorded as resolved for this brief revision by the required seat, with the affordability question answered at committed cash levels.

conditions.description: Define in advance what the pilot must show, including pilot cohort retention (currently unmeasured) and the baseline conversion comparison, plus a stop rule if participants are treated poorly or results are ambiguous.
required_evidence: Pilot plan with retention and conversion measures, thresholds, decision date, and stop rule
conditions.verification_method: Pilot plan lists measures, thresholds, a decision date, and an explicit stop rule; the plan is checked against the list before launch.

required_evidence: Named staffing and time allocation for the single pilot cohort
conditions.verification_method: Named roles and hours are attached to the pilot plan and accepted by those named.

conditions.description: Safeguard participants' dignity: tell pilot participants what they are joining, how their feedback will be used, and what happens to them when the pilot ends; do not enroll current customers without their awareness.
required_evidence: Participant communication and consent language for the pilot cohort
conditions.verification_method: Participant-facing communication and consent language are reviewed and retained before the first cohort begins.

critical_unknowns: Is the pilot affordable at committed cash levels? The brief records this financial-feasibility question as unresolved and assigns it to another seat; I make no financial determination here.
Pilot cohort retention is unmeasured, so any claim about how the revised offer serves people over time is currently unsupported.

The brief contains no evidence manifest, so no located book passage or case has been attached to this decision; the source-grounded reasoning below rests on the supplied principles, not on new evidence.
Whether the pilot's success criteria would be set by conversion alone or would include how participants were treated.
Whether the revised offer changes what customers are told or promised, which would raise the stakes of a broad launch.
Whether capacity for one cohort is genuinely available or only assumed.
decisive_arguments: The question is not only whether the revised offer converts, but what we intend by changing it and who is supposed to be served; a pilot is the smallest setting in which that intention can be checked against real experience.
The brief gives a measured baseline for the current offer (fact-1) but no measured retention for a pilot cohort (unk-1), so the honest next step is to measure rather than to scale.
Pilot capacity is an assumption (asm-1), not a fact. A bounded test is the option that surfaces whether we can carry the commitment before it becomes large.

A hard spend limit applies to both B and C (con-1), and affordability is unresolved by the seat that owns it, so the choice should be conditional on a cash-level answer rather than treated as settled.
Option C asks more people to absorb an unverified change, which is the opposite of judging the offer by how it treats the people it is meant to serve.

framework_applications.application: Adaptation, not a claim about the original text: the first move is to state plainly why we would revise the offer and who it is for, and to separate that purpose from wanting the launch to look successful. Then test whether the team actually has the capacity for even one cohort; the brief only assumes capacity, it does not establish it. Option B matches this sequence, Option C skips the purpose step and inflates the capacity requirement, Option A declines to ask the question at all.

Adaptation, not a claim about the original text: contribution is judged by present conduct and by how affected people are treated, not by rank or visibility. During a pilot that means current customers are not made to feel like test subjects, and pilot participants are told what they are joining and what happens to them afterward. Broad launch (C) removes the chance to correct treatment of people who are affected early.

option_scores.rationale: A bounded pilot is the only option that lets us name the intention behind the revised offer and then watch how it actually lands on the people it is meant to serve, before we ask a larger group to carry its consequences. It also keeps the decision inside the pilot spend already set aside, provided the affordability question is answered before money moves.

Keeping the current offer protects the measured baseline and harms no one, but it leaves the intention unanswered: we would be preserving a result rather than choosing a purpose. Status quo is defensible only if we can say what we are declining to learn and who benefits from not learning it.

A broad launch scales an untested effect on people before we know whether the revised offer serves them well; scale multiplies impact but does not create clarity about intention. It also carries the same unresolved spend constraint as the pilot with far more exposure and no measured retention.

cards.strongest_objection: A pilot can become a performance rather than a learning step: if success is defined only by conversion against the baseline, and retention is never measured, we will have spent the set-aside budget, told a small group of people they were part of something, and still be unable to say whether the revised offer genuinely serves them. Option B is only better than A or C if the purpose, the measures, and the treatment of participants are defined before the cohort starts.

cards.change_my_mind: I would move from conditional support to opposition or abstention if the source-of-funds review shows the set-aside is not surplus cash, if pilot spending would require debt or emergency reserves, if no retention measurement is defined, or if the pilot creates commitments beyond the spend cap. I would move to unqualified support for B only after affordability is evidenced and the pilot protocol, stop rules, and launch gate are fixed in writing.

conditions.description: Before any pilot spend is released, confirm that total pilot cost is fully covered by the amount already set aside and does not draw on emergency reserves, operating cash needed for obligations, or new debt.
required_evidence: Source-of-funds statement identifying the set-aside amount
Pilot cash-flow schedule including all committed costs and timing
conditions.verification_method: Review a source-of-funds statement and a full pilot cash-flow schedule signed by the finance owner.

conditions.description: Define the pilot protocol before enrollment: baseline comparator, retention metric, sample size, success threshold, stop rules, and scale-up criteria.
required_evidence: Written pilot protocol
Retention measurement plan
conditions.verification_method: Written pilot protocol reviewed by the decision owner and measurement owner.

conditions.description: Cap total pilot spend at the set-aside amount and prohibit conversion to a broad launch without a fresh affordability review and explicit launch gate.
required_evidence: Spend-cap authorization
Launch-gate checklist
conditions.verification_method: Signed spend-cap authorization and completed launch-gate checklist.

critical_unknowns: Whether the amount already set aside is genuinely surplus cash rather than emergency reserves or operating cash needed for obligations.
Whether the revised offer improves retention or only produces a temporary conversion effect.
The actual incremental costs and cash timing of the pilot, including any commitments that extend beyond the test period.
Whether the pilot capacity assumed in asm-1 is available without displacing revenue-critical work.
decisive_arguments: Option B is the only option that combines learning with a contained financial commitment, provided the pilot spend stays within the amount already set aside as required by con-1.
The current offer has a measured baseline, but pilot cohort retention is not yet measured; a bounded test converts that unknown into evidence before broader commitments.
Option C is premature because broad launch would scale spending and operational commitments before affordability and retention are established.
Financial feasibility remains unresolved, so any support for B must be conditional on a source-of-funds review, an explicit spend cap, and a launch gate.
The elder's framework treats a safety buffer as essential; a pilot that borrows from emergency reserves or creates new debt would undermine the very foundation the decision is meant to protect.

framework_applications.application: Budget-building discipline: before committing money, identify every source and use of cash and classify what is controllable. Applied here, the pilot can proceed only after the set-aside is confirmed as surplus cash and the full pilot cash-flow schedule is visible.

Save-like-a-squirrel safeguard: a safety buffer must not be raided to fund experimentation. Applied here, pilot spend must not reduce emergency savings, require new debt, or consume operating cash needed for obligations.

Action-activates-abundance discipline: take a small, tangible, measurable step rather than waiting for perfect certainty. Applied here, one bounded pilot with a fixed spend cap and predefined retention measure is preferable to either indefinite delay or an unbounded launch.

option_scores.rationale: Keeping the current offer preserves the measured baseline and avoids new spend, but it leaves the revised offer untested and does not resolve the retention unknown. From a financial-wholeness lens, standing still can be prudent, but here it forfeits a bounded, potentially informative test while the status quo already has a measured baseline.

A bounded pilot is the best fit only if it is funded entirely from the amount already set aside and does not draw on emergency reserves or create debt. It allows the team to learn retention and affordability before a broad commitment, and it turns an abstract question into a measurable, contained action. Because financial feasibility is unresolved, support must be conditional and gated by a source-of-funds check.

A broad launch commits to scale before pilot retention is measured and before affordability at committed cash levels is established. That risks destabilizing the foundation supporting the business, and it is the least consistent with a hard spend constraint and with the principle that no savings or safety buffer means a hidden debt problem.

cards.strongest_objection: Even a bounded pilot can destabilize the foundation if the amount already set aside is not truly surplus cash, if pilot activities create ongoing obligations beyond the test period, or if retention remains unmeasured. Approving a pilot without a cash-flow and source-of-funds check would risk turning a contained experiment into hidden debt or a raid on emergency savings.

cards.change_my_mind: I would move off B toward A if the reserved amount cannot fund a sample large enough to separate the revised offer from the measured baseline - an unreadable test is not a test. I would move toward a narrow version of C if a pilot read-out shows a convincing lift on both conversion and retention against the measured baseline and the budget owner confirms launch-scale spend is covered.

conditions.description: Confirm the pilot's full cash cost - media, creative, tooling, and staff time - fits inside the amount already set aside before any spend is committed, resolving the open financial feasibility question.
required_evidence: Line-item pilot budget
Confirmation of the reserved amount and that the line items fit inside it
conditions.verification_method: Line-item pilot budget reconciled against the reserved amount and signed off by the financial feasibility reviewer before the first dollar is spent.

conditions.description: Pre-register the pilot's primary success metric, the minimum lift that counts as a win against the measured baseline for the current offer, the target sample size, and the decision rule for stopping or continuing.
required_evidence: Written test plan naming the metric, minimum detectable lift, sample size, and stop/continue rule
conditions.verification_method: A dated, written test plan attached to the brief before the pilot opens and before any results are visible.

conditions.description: Name the dream customer segment and the traffic source the pilot will draw from, with expected volume, so the pilot measures the offer rather than an undefined audience.
required_evidence: Audience and traffic plan naming segment, source, and expected volume
conditions.verification_method: One-page audience and traffic plan reviewed by the marketing lead and attached to the test plan.

conditions.description: Instrument retention and follow-up measurement across the pilot cohort, because pilot cohort retention is currently unmeasured and a conversion-only read would miss the outcome most likely to differ.
required_evidence: Tracking specification covering cohort retention
Scheduled read-out date and owner
conditions.verification_method: Tracking specification approved before launch plus a scheduled read-out at a defined point after the cohort enters.

conditions.description: Set a spend stop-loss and a decision gate so that a pilot result, good or bad, is converted into an explicit launch, revise, or stop decision rather than drifting into an unbudgeted broad launch.
required_evidence: Documented stop-loss threshold
Documented launch/revise/stop decision gate
conditions.verification_method: Stop-loss threshold and decision gate documented in the test plan and acknowledged by the budget owner.

critical_unknowns: Is the pilot affordable at committed cash levels, given that the financial feasibility domain is still unresolved?
What size of lift against the measured baseline would justify a broad launch, and what size would count as a failure?
Will retention in the pilot cohort resemble retention in a launch cohort, and how long must the pilot run before that can be observed?
Which traffic source and audience segment will the pilot draw from, and is that source representative of launch traffic?
Does the revised offer change price, guarantee, delivery, or refund terms in a way that alters unit economics independent of conversion?
decisive_arguments: The brief supplies a measured baseline for the current offer and leaves pilot cohort retention unmeasured; a bounded pilot is the cheapest available mechanism to convert that gap into a measured comparison instead of an internal argument.

The hard spend constraint already caps what can be spent, so the marginal risk of piloting is small relative to the information gained, while the marginal risk of a broad launch is the full downside of scaling an untested offer.

The brief does not yet define who the revised offer is for or where those buyers are; the pilot is the correct container for naming the audience, the traffic source, and the sales path before launch-scale spend.

A pilot does not preclude a broad launch; it sequences it. Launching broadly first removes the option to learn cheaply, which is the one thing this brief's current evidence position cannot afford to lose.

framework_applications.application: The pilot should be structured so prospects vote with purchases, not with survey responses or internal approval. The measured baseline for the current offer is the comparison point; the pilot's job is to beat it or fail loudly.

Instrument the pilot across the whole path rather than the last page: lead capture, landing exchange, thank-you fulfillment, sales page, and follow-up. A pilot that only measures click-through tells us nothing about whether interest becomes a purchase.

Before spending, name the specific dream customer and the gathering place or traffic source the pilot will draw from. Without a defined audience, a pilot result cannot be attributed to the revised offer and cannot be generalized to launch traffic.
Pick the funnel shape and page order deliberately from proven patterns rather than inventing one for the pilot, so the variable under test is the offer, not the funnel architecture.

option_scores.rationale: Keeping the current offer preserves a measured baseline but converts zero new information. Standing on the known result while a revised offer sits untested buys comfort, not evidence, and the pack's coaching stance is that internal opinion about an offer is worth less than one real transaction.

A bounded pilot is the only option that produces a real market vote at capped downside. It lets the revised offer be judged against the measured baseline for the current offer, and its small scale is the natural container for defining who the buyer is, where they come from, and what the path from interest to purchase actually looks like. Score capped below 10 because affordability is unresolved and the pilot's success metric is not yet pre-registered.

Broad launch scales an unmeasured offer and an unmeasured cohort retention outcome at once. The hard spend constraint applies here as well, so a broad launch is not obviously payable, and without a pilot read-out there is no way to tell whether a good result came from the revised offer or from the audience.

cards.strongest_objection: A pilot that is underpowered or under-instrumented is worse than no pilot: it consumes the reserved budget, produces a noisy result on an unmeasured retention outcome, and invites the team to over-read a small sample as a verdict on the revised offer. If the reserved amount cannot fund a sample large enough to separate the revised offer from the measured baseline, this seat's support for B collapses toward A rather than toward C.

cards.change_my_mind: I would move away from B if the affordability check shows the pilot cannot stay within the set-aside at committed cash levels, or if no credible pre-registered test can produce a retention and conversion readout within that budget; then I would favor A until a cheaper test is designed. I would move toward C only after the pilot produces a retention readout and conversion comparison strong enough to justify broad exposure, with the affordability constraint still satisfied.

conditions.description: Before any pilot spend, produce a written cost cap and cash-flow schedule showing the pilot stays within the amount already set aside, and obtain a resolved financial-feasibility check from the designated seat.

committed-cash schedule
financial-feasibility resolution
conditions.verification_method: Finance owner signs the cost cap and cash-flow schedule; the critical-domain checker records the affordability question as resolved.

required_evidence: pre-registered pilot test plan
conditions.verification_method: Pilot lead and measurement owner sign a dated test plan before recruitment begins.

required_evidence: documented stop rules
conditions.verification_method: Stop rules are documented in the test plan and acknowledged by the accountable operator before launch.

required_evidence: participant communication draft
staff briefing note

required_evidence: pilot cohort retention readout
conversion comparison against baseline
conditions.verification_method: Measurement owner delivers a retention readout with the same cohort definition used in the test plan.

critical_unknowns: Whether the pilot can be funded inside the amount already set aside at committed cash levels.
What the pilot cohort retention rate will be.
Whether the measured baseline conversion is comparable to the pilot cohort and time period.
What specific elements of the revised offer are being tested and how success will be distinguished from novelty or seasonal effects.
How large and representative the single available cohort can be.
Whether frontline staff and participants have the capacity and support to run the pilot without hidden costs.
decisive_arguments: The brief supplies a measured baseline but does not supply pilot retention or a resolved affordability finding. A bounded pilot is the proportionate next step because it creates evidence without exposing the full market to an untested revised offer.

The hard constraint applies to both pilot and broad launch: spend must stay within the amount already set aside. That does not rule out a pilot, but it makes a written cost cap and cash-flow check a necessary condition rather than an afterthought.

Preparation is the difference between a test and an improvisation. The pilot should be pre-registered with a comparison against the baseline, a retention measure, a decision rule, and a stop rule so the organization is not later arguing over what the results mean.

Broad launch is not supported by the current brief. It would convert an unresolved retention question and an unresolved affordability question into commitments made at scale, which is the opposite of preparing holistically and protecting the people affected.
A conditional pilot respects both integrity and momentum: it does not hide the financial unknown, and it does not use that unknown as a reason to avoid learning.

framework_applications.application: Own the Story and Prepare Holistically: name plainly what is known (a measured baseline exists) and what is not (pilot retention, affordability, and the revised offer's actual performance), then over-prepare the pilot design before asking people to commit. The brief's unresolved financial-feasibility question should be confronted before execution, not discovered after spend.

Go Small on Purpose and Decode Fear: distinguish actual danger from newness. The revised offer may feel risky because it is new, but the real danger is spending outside the set-aside or scaling without a retention readout. A finite pilot with clear start and stop rules is the disciplined small action that preserves agency while the unknowns are reduced.

Go Deep, Not Broad and Institutionalize What Works: prioritize one bounded cohort with measurable outcomes instead of a broad launch. The pilot should produce documented evidence strong enough to guide a later launch decision, and it should leave behind a repeatable test protocol rather than a one-off performance.

option_scores.rationale: Keeping the current offer protects the measured baseline and avoids unverified spend, but it treats the unresolved affordability and retention questions as reasons to stand still. That is safe, not prepared; it leaves the organization without a disciplined way to learn whether the revised offer is better for the people it serves.

A bounded pilot is the strongest fit: it is a small, completable action with clear bookends, it tests the revised offer against the measured baseline before broad exposure, and it can be designed to protect participants and frontline staff. Support is conditional because the financial-feasibility domain is unresolved and the pilot spend must stay within the amount already set aside.

Broad launch outruns the evidence. The brief says the baseline is measured, but pilot cohort retention is not yet measured and affordability is unresolved. Launching broadly would ask the most people to absorb unverified risk while the organization is still missing the facts needed for a responsible decision.

cards.strongest_objection: The pilot itself may be imprudent if the set-aside is already committed or too small to fund a clean test. A half-funded pilot can produce weak evidence, consume cash, and delay the harder decision; in that case the organization should not run the pilot merely to appear decisive.

cards.change_my_mind: I would move toward C if audited cash availability shows broad launch is within the set-aside, retention evidence already exists at adequate confidence, and a pre-registered readout shows no incremental learning from a pilot. I would move toward A if affordability cannot be confirmed or the pilot cannot be isolated without contaminating the baseline.

critical_unknowns: Is the pilot affordable at committed cash levels, as the unresolved financial_feasibility domain asks?
What retention result would count as success or failure, and what sample is needed to read it?
What difficult customer or team conversation is being avoided by moving to a broad launch?
Can the pilot cohort be isolated without harming the measured baseline?
Who has authority to stop the pilot if spend or retention guardrails are breached?
decisive_arguments: fact-1 establishes a measured baseline, but unk-1 says pilot cohort retention is not yet measured; broad launch C would scale before the key learning exists.
con-1 is a hard budget constraint for B and C; a trustworthy pilot must first answer the finance question rather than treat the set-aside as elastic.

The avoided conversation is likely not 'pilot or launch' but 'what evidence are we willing to accept, who owns the cash answer, and what would make us stop?' Clear is kind requires writing those boundaries down.
B is the only option that pairs courage with boundaries: it exposes the revised offer to real customers in a limited way while protecting the baseline and the budget.
A is safer than an unfunded or unmeasured pilot, but as a default it avoids the vulnerable action of testing and learning.

framework_applications.application: Atlas Method: precise naming. The team should name the actual uncertainty—retention evidence, cash affordability, or fear of a negative result—before choosing a pilot or launch; vague urgency hides the specific risk.

BRAVING and boundaries: trust is built by explicit boundaries—pilot budget, cohort, duration, stop rules, and reporting. Without those boundaries, a pilot becomes unkind ambiguity and a broad launch becomes unbounded exposure.

Clear is kind and rumble with vulnerability: the avoided conversation is about limits and evidence. Trustworthy leadership asks finance for a hard affordability answer and tells customers and the team what is and is not being decided.

Only option that creates bounded learning before scale: it can respect con-1 if affordability is verified, test the revised offer against the measured baseline, and replace unk-1 with evidence. It also forces the avoided conversation about cash, success criteria, and stop rules.

Broad launch scales an offer while retention is unmeasured and financial feasibility is unresolved. It converts a hard constraint into an after-the-fact hope and performs confidence rather than practicing trustworthy leadership.

cards.strongest_objection: A pilot can become a way to delay a hard decision while spending scarce cash; if affordability or clean measurement is not secured, B is worse than A.

framework_applications.application: Law 7 ('Make thy money grow') requires investing only in what you understand; the revised offer is not yet understood at any measured level, so the pilot is the instrument of understanding and broad launch would be investing blind. The disciplines of clarity and persistence applied together mean the pilot must have a written definition of success and a fixed measurement window; a pilot without pre-registered thresholds is not discipline, it is drift with a budget line.

Knowledge + Action + Commitment = Empowerment. The brief supplies a partial knowledge base (a measured baseline for the current offer) and names the missing piece (pilot retention). The pilot is the action step that tests commitment against reality, at a size where a setback is tuition rather than catastrophe.

Courage is action in the presence of fear, not absence of it. Launching broadly to avoid the discomfort of measuring is not courage but a gamble; running the bounded test and reading the result honestly is the disciplined form of the same courage.

option_scores.rationale: Keeping the current offer preserves a measured baseline but buys no new knowledge. The brief leaves the pilot cohort's retention unmeasured (unk-1) and the revised offer unmeasured; choosing stillness is not the same as choosing discipline, because a known-but-unexamined baseline still leaves the larger opportunity untested and no capability is built.

A bounded test is the one path that turns an unknown into knowledge at survivable cost. It fits the discipline of investing only in what you understand and of making money grow from measured ground rather than from hope. My support is conditional, not unconditional: the pilot must be pre-registered with success thresholds, a named end date, and a cash envelope confirmed against con-1 by the financial-feasibility seat.

Broad launch commits capital, reputation, and operating attention to an offer whose results have not been measured. That is the opposite of the discipline of understanding what you invest in; it converts activity into spend before the business owns the learning. If pilot evidence later replicates with margin intact, my score for C rises sharply, but not before.

cards.strongest_objection: The pilot as scoped may not retire the decisive unknown. That is a real risk, and it is why my support is conditional on pre-registered retention thresholds rather than on the pilot label itself.

I would move to keeping the current offer if the financial check showed the pilot is unaffordable or if the team cannot instrument retention; a real constraint is a constraint, not a belief to be pushed through.
